So if we could have the Registrar distribute this master list as well as ... once this is distributed, Your Honour, I will explain what you have received. Your Honours and counsel have received two documents. Let me refer first to the thicker of the two documents. This is a document, Your Honour, that is a master list of Mr. Randall's exhibits. It -- let me orient you through this. On the left-hand side is the 65 ter number, followed by a short description. The English and ERN, English and B/C/S ERN, and then there's a column with the source of the document. And in the far right-hand column there is a column identifying the protective measures. For ease of reference, for everybody in the courtroom, this document has shaded items, and the items that are shaded are protected, either in whole or in part. So both these documents, hopefully will be of assistance to the Court and to the witness. Now, I do request, Your Honour, that this master list be made available to Mr. Randall during his testimony because when I asked him about the provenance of a document he will need to refer to this list in order to recall specifically what the provenance of the document is. Likewise, I would also ask that this exhibit collection schedule, the two-page item, likewise be made available to Mr. Randall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now in attempting to manage this many documents, what I intend to do, and with leave of the Court, I intend to exhibit some of the documents; in other words I intend to call up on the screen some of the exhibits. There are, however, many exhibits that are similar in type or in theme. So if, for example, we take SDC minutes, what I propose to do is to exhibit one such set of minutes from a session, and then I have prepared schedules with the remaining similar documents, identified both by session, and source. And what I would propose to do is -- and prior to seeking the admission of the items on the schedule, I would distribute to the Chamber and to the parties a schedule with the items for which I'm seeking admission. The schedules are essentially similar to what is on the master list but filtered to reflect only the items that are relevant to the schedule. So dealing SDC minutes, for example, you would have a filtered of the minutes which would identify 65 ter numbers down the side. The list is helpful, I think, to permit the Trial Chamber quickly to see what items the Prosecution is seeking admission of, to quickly identify the sources of those items, and for the Registrar to quickly be able to make references to what needs to be marked as an exhibit and what doesn't -- what is protected and what is partially protected. What I would do, Your Honour, is distribute the schedules prior to asking the witness questions about those particular items. The use of the schedules, I think, Your Honour, will permit me to get through large numbers of documents of similar origin or similar types, or in the case of themes, similar thematic content.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Have you discussed this procedure with your colleagues on the opposite side?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, there has been some discussion. Are you -- I'm picking up an echo, just a minute. See if you turn it down, see if that will help. Well, that's better. We have had some discussion about the utilisation of schedules as a methodology for the introduction of documents. At this juncture since we haven't had an opportunity to have a truly meaningful discussion with Mr. Harmon concerning this matter, I think it would be fair to say that with regard to certain specific subjects or types of documents - for example, the SDC minutes - we are in agreement as regards to those documents. With regards to other documents, we may be running into a problem, in terms of using this particular kind of methodology. However, I think it would be fair to say that with regard to at least a number of those exhibits that the Prosecution wishes to introduce through the schedule methodology, that's what I'll call it for the moment, we are in accord and it will be no difficulty. And I think we will be able to tighten that up as things goes on. This is going to take, I believe, a considerable period of time because there are -- it would be fair to say there are thousands of documents that are going to be coming through Mr. Randall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON

We are mindful of the fact that we should not be running over each other's areas, nor do we wish to tag team Mr. Harmon in any fashion whatsoever in this regard. utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated. Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Randall could you state your name please and spell your last name for the record.

utterances.speaker: BRETTON RANDALL
utterances.text: My name is Bretton Randall. My family name is spelled R-a-n-d-a-l-l.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Randall, I'm going to read to you, your background, and I would ask you to affirm if what I have read is accurate.

utterances.speaker: BRETTON RANDALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. You graduated in 1982 from the Victoria Police Constable's course in Melbourne, Australia. You were with the Uniform Police Service in Victoria until 1987. In 1989 you graduated from the Victoria Police detective training school. You were a detective for the Victoria Police from 1988 until January 2001. You investigated cases of murder, rape, armed robbery, aggravated burglary, kidnapping, extortion, drug trafficking, drug importation, money laundering, corruption, foreign incursions, and fraud. For ten years you specialized in investigating crimes including organised crime involving or related to South East Asian community. Between 1996 and 2000, you were seconded to the National Crime Authority, a multi-jurisdictional, multi-disciplinary federal criminal investigative body during which time you investigated domestic and international drug importation, money laundering, and corruption relating to the South East Asian community. You commenced your duties as an investigator in the Office of the Prosecutor at the ICTY on 9 February 2001. And you remained in that capacity until you left on the 16th of November 2008. You are currently employed at the ICC as an investigator with the Office of the Prosecutor. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRETTON RANDALL
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Randall, first let me begin by focussing your attention on procedures at the ICTY. Can you describe to the Chamber the procedure that is utilized in collecting evidence and the chain of custody.

utterances.speaker: BRETTON RANDALL
utterances.text: Well, once evidence comes into the custody of the Office of the Prosecutor, it is then registered within the evidence unit, and by that, the source of the evidence, the date it was received, from whom it was received, a description is then entered. This is all done on an evidence registration form. Any other pertinent information, if there was in the caveats attached to it that were -- may have been applied at the time of the provision. That -- a document is then allocated a specific number. That is then taken -- printed in hard copy. It's attached to the evidence itself. It's then taken to the evidence unit where it is registered within the evidence unit. The unique number which is the identifier for that specific piece of evidence is entered into a document, and then the evidence is then handed over to the evidence unit. Once it is it in the evidence unit they then deal with the processing of the evidence which includes, if it is a document for example, allocating an ERN number, stamping it. It is then taken and put into -- is retained in possession of the evidence unit and stored in the custody vaults.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, can you also describe as part of your duties, did you participate in analysing documentation from which requests for assistance were disseminated?

utterances.speaker: BRETTON RANDALL
utterances.text: Yes, did I.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you describe briefly the Request for Assistance process.

utterances.speaker: BRETTON RANDALL
utterances.text: Well, Request for Assistance is generated when an avenue of inquiry is identified and that request can manifest itself in a number of ways, can be sent to either a country or to a government or to a particular international institution such as Interpol. An analysis is -- in summary analysis of material is conducted, from that an objective is identified. We may request that a particular government issue a waiver for a particular person, identify a particular person, provide documents. It can relate to a number of different issues. The request is then drafted usually that is done by members of the investigations division, but at the time, also by some of the legal team. It can also be from the military analysis team, leadership research, for example. It is drafted. It is then sent to the Senior Trial Attorney for approval, and if approved, it is then sent to the Prosecutor for signature usually. Although at times the Senior Trial Attorneys have also signed some of the these requests; they're then forwarded to the respective government or institution. Usually we would set a time -- a particular time-frame for a response depending on what the request was. The average time that we allowed was generally four to six weeks. If there was no response within that particular time, usually a reminder would be sent to the government or the institution, seeking -- seeking a response. Then a response would come back, and at times that would involve the provision of certain documents, for example, and within an accompanying letter that would then come back to the Office of the Prosecutor, usually to the investigators, and the investigators were then responsible for then entering the data into the -- as I described earlier and submitting -- submitting the documents or the evidence to the evidence unit for securing the process.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What would happen if there was non-compliance with the request?

utterances.speaker: BRETTON RANDALL
utterances.text: Well the options would be discussed among the team. One would be to avail ourself to the use of Rule of 54 bis, but prior to doing that, the usual process would be to - depending on where the -- to which institution or country the request was sent to - if it was sent to, for example, Serbia or Bosnia, we would ask the head of mission to make approaches to the government and ascertain, you know, when we would expect to receive a response, and hopefully that would be sufficient to prompt a response. If not, then often the Prosecutor would be involved and he would make a representation on behalf of the -- of the Prosecution. And if that was -- if that didn't wasn't successful in obtaining an adequate response, because quite often we would receive a response and it may not be adequate for our understanding, we would then -- well, we would then avail ourself to Rule 54 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could ask that Mr. Randall be provided with the master list that I showed you earlier, and the exhibit collection schedule, two-page document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Randall, you have seen both of those items before coming into court. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRETTON RANDALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. You can use -- can you use those items for reference when I ask you about the source of certain documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Harmon, I do apologise. But looking at the exhibit list, we have 65 ter 05020, and then the next document is 05047. So we may be making a mistake. We find that on page 70. If it might be of some help, I believe this has also been previously admitted into evidence as Exhibit 196.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If this is a previous exhibit, then I will withdraw this exhibit. There's no need for Mr. Randall to testify about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 5612 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON

utterances.speaker: BRETTON RANDALL

utterances.text: And this is handover of duty to what -- in what capacity?

utterances.speaker: BRETTON RANDALL
utterances.text: Colonel General Perisic relinquishing his post to Colonel General Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I would ask, Your Honour, that this be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P702, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 5089 on the monitor, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is -- this is a document, Mr. Randall, that is a FRY Presidential Decree dated the 24th November 1998. It is signed by President Slobodan Milosevic, relating to the deployment and appointment of General Perisic. Can you identify the source of this document?

utterances.speaker: BRETTON RANDALL
utterances.text: From memory, I believe that was provided when we requested provision of VJ personnel file of the accused. I'm not sure which request number it relates to but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You care to refer to the master list in front of you and be more specific?

utterances.speaker: BRETTON RANDALL
utterances.text: What was the 65 ter again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I suggest, Mr. Randall, that you refer to Mr. Perisic as Mr. Perisic and not the accused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It was received from the government of Serbia and Montenegro in response to our request to our Request for Assistance, number 1034.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If that that be given an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So given. May it please be given a name.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P703, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 5613 on the monitor, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Randall, 5613 is a Presidential Decree dated the 12th of March 1999. It is signed by President Milosevic, and it is the termination of professional military service of Momcilo Perisic. Can you identify the source of this document, please?

utterances.speaker: BRETTON RANDALL

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a problem because the B/C/S version of the document does not correspond to the English version. The document that is being shown in B/C/S is the previous document that was looked at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we mark this for identification, Your Honour, for the moment, and unless there's a -- just one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For your information, the document in e-court, how we received it on the hyperlink for the 65 ter network, actually, does not correspond. What I'm trying to say is that we did not receive the B/C/S version of the document that Mr. Harmon is looking at now, and that's ERN number 06006005. We would like to receive the correct document in B/C/S so that we can look at it, and then hopefully we will have objection to the document, and I think it's fine for to be MFIed right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We'll make sure the proper page is uploaded into e-court. So if it could be given a number, it could be MFIed, and then we will upload the proper page during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we give that an exhibit number, marked for identification, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P704, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Also, if I might, before we get too far down the road here, and I understand that Mr. Randall is identifying that he received these documents from specific sources and has -- and has described for us thus far both the chain of custody and RFA process. But rather than stand up each time and interpose a potential relevance objection to the document that is being admitted either individually or when we reach the issue of groups of documents, I -- I question at this time what is the purpose of the introduction of these documents, since Mr. Randall was speaking to a very specific issue. That is, the question of source, as opposed to the issue of the truth of the contents of the documents themselves. I'm asking at this point, so that we don't get into difficulty as we go along. And I figure at the outset it's an issue that perhaps needs to be addressed. Mr. Harmon may feel the same or he may feel differently; I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Randall is identifying the source of these documents. If there is an issue on the relevancy of these documents, obviously that is a separate objection; it can be raise; we can address it. If there are relevancy objections tor the documents, rather than addressing each of the documents individually in the process of presenting this many documents, I would suggest that we identify documents for which there is an relevancy objection at the conclusion of Mr. Randall' evidence, that we make submissions as to the relevance of each of the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It seems to me that you are at cross-purposes with your colleague. It looks like your colleague is talking about the truthfulness of the contents of the documents rather than the relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I don't understand the objection, Your Honour. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might, so there is no misunderstanding, the fact that the gentleman can identify a document in and of itself may be of some use to the Chamber. But I assume that it is the Prosecution's intent in the future to rely on the contents of the document, as opposed to the fact that Mr. Randall can identify the document, the actual contents that are contained in the document for the purposes of asserting particular legal and factual arguments. So that extent they're going to be relying on what is the truth of the documents contained -- what is the truth of the matters that are contained within the documents. My assumption, and perhaps I'm mistaken, is that Mr. Harmon is going have some witness to connect all of these documents up with some issues that are in fact relevant to the issues before the Chamber. Otherwise, the document in and of itself has no relevance, if it is to be considered outside of the information that's contained therein, which is why I asked the question, what is the purpose of introducing these documents. Does that clarify my concern? I mean, that's the first issue. Because I don't know want to be in a situation where there is any misunderstanding here. Because if I don't know what the purpose is of the proffer document, then I'm not in a position to challenge the relevancy of the document. And rather than get into a situation where we get used to the wholesale introduction of documents by virtue that Mr. Randall is in a position to recognise the document itself, I think we should probably have some clarification here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, these are records that were received from the state. They are records that we are introducing for the truth of the their contents. The relevance of these documents establish what is identified in the indictment as when Mr. Perisic began his duties as chief of the General Staff, and when he ended his duties as the chief of the General Staff. So we are offering these documents for the truth of the content.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, understanding that position, I believe it raises a couple of problems. The first problem is that, unless the Prosecution can establish some linkage between the document and the witness testifying, apart from the fact that he received the document, then it is in violation of the guidelines that we are to proceeding under. Now, as I understand the purpose of Mr. Randall's testimony he essentially operates as a chain of custody witness; nothing more, and nothing less. Two --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And was not in terms of a decision of the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Fair enough. So ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That does not deal with the next issue, which is if the Chamber receives a document, whatever document it may be, and Mr. Randall operates as a chain of custody witness, that does not attend to the issue of the contents of the document itself. That's a different issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... Chamber decided, so -- and I think the Prosecution is proceeding according to the decision of the Chamber. And so be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

I didn't feel the need to display this particular exhibit, but if Your Honours wish that the first page of this be -- publicly displayed, I'm happy to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, it's just that when you depart from normal procedure, do let us know. The normal procedure is that before you tender any document or any exhibit, we first see it. So if you -- if you are going to depart at least forewarn us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON

So I'm concerned that with the speed of tendering the documents something may be admitted that might turn out to have a problem with the English translation which will crop up later. And I believe that if it is an important mistake, it's something that we could, through dealing with the witnesses or the interpreters, could be corrected. But perhaps I can speak with Mr. Harmon and then for certain documents we have no objections to, we could inform jointly the Trial Chamber about it, and then perhaps the Chamber could agree to tender these documents in that way and discuss only documents to which we might have an objection of a legal nature or some other grounds. And I don't know, perhaps Mr. Guy-Smith would like to add something.

Something came to my mind as we were sitting here that might work in terms of getting the information to you in a more efficient manner. At least so it goes from this side of the room to that side of the room. If -- and I don't know whether or not we can do that rapidly, meaning within the next few minutes or whether that is going to take perhaps a couple of hours of conferencing as between the Prosecution and Defence, but that may be well of a manner of spending the time well and ultimately saving a fair amount of court time from the standpoint of what we're doing here. But I would like to underscore that again with the fact there are some both global as well as specific underlying legal issues that we do have some concerns about. So I don't want to be in a position where -- I'm sorry, Your Honour, I didn't mean to interrupt. But I don't want to be in a position whereby going through this particular method, we have waived any substantive legal concerns that we may have.
